Friday Coding Kickoff

Today is Friday, March 27, 2026. Let's look at the actual code patterns that make Spring Boot feel like magic.

1. Creating a REST Endpoint

The bread and butter of Spring Boot. Use @RestController to tell Spring this class handles HTTP requests, and @GetMapping to map a specific URL path to a method.

2. Path Variables

Used to capture dynamic values directly from the URL path. This is standard for fetching specific resources, like an item ID in a retail POS system.

3. Request Parameters

Captured from the query string (the part after the ? in a URL). Useful for filtering, sorting, or searching through product lists.

4. Handling POST Data

When sending data to the server (like a new user or order), use @PostMapping and @RequestBody. Spring automatically converts the incoming JSON into a Java object.

5. Constructor Injection

The modern, recommended way to perform Dependency Injection. It makes your code easier to test and ensures required dependencies aren't null.

6. Reading Properties

Use the @Value annotation to pull specific configuration values from your application.properties or application.yml file.

7. Defining a Service Layer

Keep your controllers 'thin' by putting business logic in @Service classes. This keeps your code clean, modular, and reusable.

8. Creating a Data Repository

With Spring Data JPA, you don't write SQL. Just extend JpaRepository and Spring provides all the CRUD operations (save, delete, find) for you.

9. Global Exception Handling

Instead of messy try-catch blocks in every method, use @RestControllerAdvice to catch specific exceptions globally and return a clean error message.

10. Running Code on Startup

The CommandLineRunner interface is perfect for running logic (like seeding a database or logging system status) immediately after the app starts.

Friday Coding Deep-Dive

Today is Friday, March 27, 2026. Let's explore the intermediate patterns that turn a basic Spring Boot app into a production-grade service.

1. Mocking Beans in Tests (@MockBean)

When writing integration tests, you often need to mock external services (like a payment gateway). @MockBean replaces a real bean in the Spring Context with a Mockito mock.

2. Profile-Specific Configuration

Spring Boot allows you to define different settings for different environments using the application-{profile}.yml naming convention. You can toggle between dev, test, and prod easily.
code:
# application-dev.yml
server:
  port: 8081

# application-prod.yml
server:
  port: 80

body:
3. Scheduling Tasks (@Scheduled)

Used to execute tasks at fixed intervals or specific times (cron expressions). Perfect for daily reports, clearing cache, or processing retail batches.

4. Asynchronous Methods (@Async)

Allows methods to run in a separate background thread. The caller doesn't have to wait for the method to finish, which improves the responsiveness of your API.

5. Custom Actuator Health Indicators

You can extend the HealthIndicator interface to add your own health checks (e.g., checking if an external API is reachable) to the `/actuator/health` endpoint.

6. Bean Validation (@NotBlank, @Size)

Use Hibernate Validator annotations on your DTOs to enforce data integrity. Spring automatically checks these when a request hits your Controller.

7. Spring Interceptors

HandlerInterceptor allows you to perform actions before or after a request is handled by a controller. Useful for logging, authentication checks, or adding headers.

8. Database Migrations (Flyway)

Tools like Flyway or Liquibase manage your database schema changes. They run SQL scripts on startup to ensure your database structure matches your code.
code:
// Script: V1__create_users_table.sql
CREATE TABLE users (id INT, name VARCHAR(50));

body:
9. @ConditionalOnProperty

Used to conditionally load a bean only if a specific property is set in the configuration. This is the foundation for Feature Toggles.

10. Enabling CORS Support

If your front-end and back-end are on different domains, use @CrossOrigin to allow the browser to make requests to your Spring Boot API.

11. Lazy Initialization (@Lazy)

By default, Spring beans are eagerly initialized at startup. Using @Lazy delays the creation of a bean until it is actually needed, which can speed up application startup.

12. Customizing the Banner

You can replace the default Spring logo at startup with custom ASCII art by placing a banner.txt file in the resources folder.

13. Repository Testing (@DataJpaTest)

A specialized test annotation that only loads the JPA components, providing an in-memory database and configured EntityManager for fast repository testing.

14. Logging Levels and Logback

Spring Boot uses Logback by default. You can control the verbosity (TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR) for specific packages in your properties file.
code:
logging:
  level:
    org.springframework: ERROR
    com.myapp: DEBUG

body:
15. Graceful Shutdown

Ensures that when the application stops, it finishes processing active requests before shutting down the server. This prevents data loss or broken connections.
code:
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s
